questions: Has the affected eye developed any new loss or blurring of vision?
Do you have severe pain in or around the affected eye?
Does moving the affected eye cause pain?
Did the swelling or bruising begin suddenly?
Did it follow any injury, fall, assault, surgery, injection, or vigorous rubbing of the eye?
Has the swelling or bruising been rapidly worsening?
Have you had a severe headache, nausea, or vomiting?
Has one pupil become noticeably larger than the other?
Does the affected eye appear pushed forward or unable to move normally?
Have you developed weakness, numbness, confusion, trouble speaking, or difficulty walking?
Are the eyelids or surrounding skin markedly red, hot, or draining pus?
Have you recently started a new medication or had an insect bite or other allergic exposure?
Do you take blood thinners or have a bleeding or bruising disorder?
Have you had similar unexplained eye swelling or bruising before?
Do you have thyroid disease or a history of orbital or eye problems?
orders: Measure visual acuity in each eye separately.
Examine pupils and perform a swinging-flashlight test for a relative afferent pupillary defect.
Test extraocular movements in all directions and assess for pain, restriction, or diplopia.
Perform slit-lamp examination with fluorescein staining.
Measure intraocular pressure in each eye.
Examine the eyelids, conjunctiva, and surrounding facial skin for dermatitis, urticaria, excoriations, and signs of infection.
Examine the rest of the skin and mucous membranes for bruising, petechiae, or angioedema.
Complete blood count with platelet count.
Prothrombin time/INR and activated partial thromboplastin time.
Comprehensive metabolic panel, including liver and kidney function.

Alternative: Allergic contact dermatitis of the eyelids

Alternative: Occult periorbital trauma

Alternative: Early periorbital cellulitis or other inflammatory orbital process
